[[RunningHead]]

From the details of the individual to the tendencies of the species: Both clinical reports and affective neuroscience enrich the neuropsychoanalytic dialogue

Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

New York City
The Neuropsychoanalysis Foundation

Maggie Zellner  

One of the most valuable things about neuropsychoanalysis is the way in which the “vehicles” of our dialogue – neuroscientific and psychoanalytic ideas and data – shine new light in both directions as they drive the now rather wide highway emerging between the two domains. Neurological observations illuminate theoretical propositions from psychoanalysis; likewise, psychoanalytic concepts and rich clinical wisdom create new points of contact with neuroscientific research. The pieces in this issue of Neuropsychoanalysis all exemplify this trend in various ways.

In their article “The Impact of Traumatic Brain Injury on Awareness and Mourning: the Role of Concrete Behavior,” Christian Salas and Rudi Coetzer travel this neuropsychoanalytic highway in both directions with nuance and range. They discuss the frequent presentation of concrete behavior in patients who have survived traumatic brain injury (TBI); this concrete behavior seems to arise from damage to circuits which mediate memory and prediction, so that patients are left in a vivid here-and-now with diminished capacity to reflect, and at the same time seem to have an impaired capacity to mourn, which often impedes the process of adjusting to their new circumstances. Clearly the dysregulation of brain and mind are interwoven here: the underlying circuits required for reflection and grieving may be structurally affected, and at the same time the psychodynamic need to protect the self from the pain of loss may be magnified by the very loss the person has suffered.

Salas and Coetzer also remind us about a use of the term “default mode” in behavioral neurology that is almost completely opposite its current sense in the emerging literature on “resting state” brain networks. With this term, Mesulam (2002) described a mode of concrete, here-and-now functioning that predominates when the capacity for abstraction is impaired following damage to certain cortical functions. Mesulam's meaning stands in intriguing contrast to the current linkage of activity of the “default mode network” with daydreaming or “stimulus-independent thought,” which is the aspect of conscious mental life that is the most removed from here-and-now perception (see, for example,Andrews-Hanna, Smallwood, & Spreng, 2014). Future work could productively explore this bifurcated application of the same term – what kinds of functioning do humans “default” to, and under what conditions? The functioning that Salas and Coetzer describe in TBI survivors, who appear to be stuck in a concrete “default mode” sheds light on the importance of symbolization and fantasy in affect regulation, which has both positive and negative short-term effects, as readers will see when reading the sensitive clinical vignettes in their piece.

Maladaptive defense mechanisms are associated with decoupling of testosterone from sexual desire in women of reproductive age

Rui Costa and Rui Oliveira

Rui Oliveira

Rui Oliveira  

maladaptive defense mechanisms, testosterone, female sexual desire, alexithymia, decoupling of testosterone from reported sexual desire

Neuropsychoanalytic theories view maladaptive defense mechanisms as disturbances of brain regions or networks implicated in emotional awareness, which is consistent with maladaptive defenses being automatic processes to cope with stressors by avoiding the awareness of disturbing emotions. Freud proposed that defenses against sexual drives were used in varying degrees with negative consequences on sex life, which is congruent with maladaptive defenses being related to lower desire for vaginal intercourse. The present study examined the relationships between low desire, maladaptive defenses, and decoupling of testosterone (T; a hormonal index of sexual desire) from reported desire. Sixty-eight Portuguese women provided a saliva sample before and 15 minutes after an induction of sexual fantasy, and reported how much sexual desire they felt while fantasizing. Maladaptive defenses were measured by the immature defenses subscale of the Defense Style Questionnaire (DSQ-40). Past month desire was assessed by the desire domain of the Female Sexual Function Index. Luminescence immunoassays were used for determining salivary T. Decoupling of T from desire was calculated by the absolute value of the subtraction of the standardized scores of both measures. In partial correlations controlling for social desirability and oral contraception, maladaptive defenses correlated with discordance between basal T and fantasy-induced desire, discordance between basal T and past month desire, and complaints of low desire. In a backward multiple regression, discordance between T and past month desire explained the association between maladaptive defenses and complaints of low desire. Implications for future neuropsychoanalytic studies of defense mechanisms and libido are discussed.

Daniela Flores Mosri

Daniela Flores Mosri   *Email: dannmos@yahoo.com

The 16th Annual Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society took place in Amsterdam during July 9–11, 2015, followed by a Sunday post-congress discussion on July 12th. The Congress was held at the University of Amsterdam and the Sunday meeting at the Psychoanalytic Foundation. People from all regions of the world attended, including countries such as Japan, Israel, Turkey, Panama, Finland, Puerto Rico, Spain, South Africa and Suriname among many others, constituting a widely varied community of people interested in neuropsychoanalysis.

As seen in previous congresses, an educational day preceded the official start of the Congress with four speakers. The first was Anna Bentinck van Schoonheten, who spoke about changes in personality, repetition and psychoanalytic technique in the history of psychoanalysis. Her talk reviewed some of Freud's reflections about the objectives of the psychoanalytic technique, going from discovering unconscious material and communicating it at the right moment to the patient by means of interpretation, to the limitations of psychoanalytic treatments by admitting that the patient is unable to remember all the repressed material that could be of relevance to the treatment. The importance of the transference was highlighted, in order to review some of the concepts in Kleinian theory such as the role of introjection and projection and their differences in pregenital and genital patients. The next talk was given by Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber with a presentation entitled How to study the outcomes of psychoanalyses? A balancing act between societal needs and epistemological impossibilities. Leuzinger-Bohleber specified the complexities around psychoanalytical research in detail and also described her ongoing psychoanalytic project on depression. After comparing cognitive–behavioral long-term therapies against psychoanalysis, the outcome was shown to be the same with either technique. Symptoms diminished after one year of treatment but psychoanalyses also had the chance of recording important data related to the patients' depression. These data revealed that childhood trauma was found in about 85% of the participants. Furthermore, dreams were used to observe the progress of the patients and they changed over the course of treatment: they came to include more human than animal characters, the patient was more active and the most important person in the dream, and affects grew in intensity.

Research and Symposia Abstracts from the Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, 2015

The 16th Annual Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, Amsterdam, July 9-11, 2015: “Plasticity and Repetition (and Other Topics)”

At our 16th annual congress, the development of neuropsychoanalytic research came into view more clearly than ever. Colleagues from around the world presented on a diverse range of topics in research sessions and symposia, using a range of methods. Sensitive clinical work with patients with brain injury was presented in parallel with neurophysiology findings on sleep and dreams. Neuroscience experiments that addressed psychoanalytic constructs like repression and object relations were presented alongside animal work on memory processes and development.

As an audience member who has been present at all of our research days since our first one in Stockholm in 2002 (which featured just eight pioneering researchers), it was deeply satisfying to see this explosion of serious and nuanced work emerging from all corners of the globe. Even more exciting was the number of young, bright researchers throwing their hats in the ring. It was wonderful to see so many people entering this neuropsychoanalytic dialogue from the beginning of their training, with such enthusiasm and thoughtfulness. Indeed, the very matter-of-factness with which they are integrating the two domains indicates that our interdisciplinary endeavor has truly taken off.

To get a full sense of the ground covered at this congress, read the abstracts in this section. Then keep your eyes out for the published papers that are bound to follow, both in these pages and in other scientific journals. We thank our dedicated congress co-hosts at RINO-Noord Holland for their incredible support in running the conference in Amsterdam. We also encourage you to submit proposals for our next congress in Chicago, in July 2016; stay tuned for details!

In his foreword to this book, Mark Solms colorfully describes his first day as a neuropsychologist at a neurosurgical ward, and how difficult it was for him then, when this book did not exist yet. Solms's story reminded me of my first weeks as a neuropsychologist of a neurological rehabilitation ward. I remember buying Neuropsychological assessment by Muriel D. Lezak, which was (and I think still is) considered “the bible” of the field. I was determined to read it all, chapter by chapter, in order to learn everything there was to know about neuropsychology from the very beginning of my life as a clinician. However, the impossible length (some 1000 pages) of Lezak's book, combined with my intensive clinical work, made me give up on my ambitious (if not obsessive) project after three chapters.

Since then, Lezak's book has become a good professional friend and an endless source of information for specific questions. However, upon reflection, some more manageable, friendly reading material could have definitely helped me with the difficult, sometimes overwhelming transition from being a university student to being a full-time clinician working with brain-injured patients. Coetzer and Balchin's new book does a wonderful job responding to this challenge. The book's 200 pages offer a compact, yet comprehensive and pleasant reading experience, which prepares the reader for the task of working with patients who suffer from brain lesions.

In the preface, the authors describe clinical neuropsychology as “a curious beast, representing equal measures of science and art”, and propose that “neuropsychology can be very technical on the one hand, but can also demand extraordinary humanity and compassion on the other”. One of the big achievements of this book is its success in representing both sides of this “curious beast” very well. The book nicely covers the relevant, essential aspects of “brain-behavior relations science” on the one hand, and sensitively and respectfully deals with the clinical art of work with brain-injured patients on the other. Encompassing almost all aspects of clinical neuropsychology within these two broad categories of (neuro) science and (clinical) art in one short book is no small accomplishment.

Is concreteness the invisible link between altered emotional processing, impaired awareness and mourning difficulties after traumatic brain injury?

Christian E. Salas and Rudi Coetzer

Rudi Coetzer

Colwyn Bay
UK
North Wales Brain Injury Service

UK
Centre for Rehabilitation, Faculty of Health and Life Sciences

Manchester
UK

Rudi Coetzer  

awareness, mourning, concrete behavior, emotion, traumatic brain injury, self-psychology

Deficits in awareness are a common problem after traumatic brain injury (TBI), often compromising the process of emotional adjustment, including mourning. Unfortunately, there is little understanding of how the specific profile of cognitive impairment and emotional change often presented by individuals with TBI influences awareness and mourning. Concrete behavior has been often described as a feature of TBI, with a difficulty detaching from immediate experience (both internal and external) as its signature. From a self-psychology perspective, concrete behavior can be understood as a change in the cohesion and structure of the self, where temporal and representational domains are modified. This paper offers a novel approach to problems of awareness and mourning after TBI, by considering how temporal and representational changes in the phenomenology of the self alter individuals' emotional landscape. More specifically, it describes how concreteness modifies several aspects of emotional life that are central to awareness and mourning, such as emotional reactivity, emotional regulation, emotional understanding, and signal anxiety. The impact that concreteness has in awareness and mourning is also discussed in detail throughout the paper, as well as the technical challenges implied. Finally, some general guidelines to address changes in the phenomenology of the self in a therapeutic context are briefly described.

This edition of our group reports from the world of neuropsychoanalysis presents some additional reasons for you to join in!

Our first Regional Bulletin editor, Irene Mathis, gives us a great summing-up of the intense work they keep going in Sweden. Similarly, the intensity of work and enthusiasm of Daniela Flores Mosri from the Neuropsychoanalysis Group in Mexico City and of Gökçe Özkarar-Gradwohl from the Turkish Neuropsychoanalysis Study Group makes me feel enthusiastic about the seeds we planted at the founding of our Society in the year 2000 – with these groups we are seeing the results of it! And last but not least, new groups have joined us – giving us reason enough to carry on: a group in Puerto Rico led by Efrain J. Rios-Ruiz, and the Polish Neuropsychoanalysis Study Group led by Slawomir Murawiec. We look forward to tracking the developments of these new colleagues.

msonia12@gmail.com

The London Neuropsychoanalysis Group

The London Neuropsychoanalysis group is now in its seventh year, with a strong membership of about 130 professionals and students from several regions within the UK.

We are an interdisciplinary group of mostly “mid-career” neuropsychologists and neuroscientists, as well as some analysts, psychotherapists, psychiatrists and philosophers with an interest in different psychoanalytic models. Katerina Fotopoulou set up this group four years ago with Diana Caine, with the aim of creating a supportive, free, educational platform where we can exchange perspectives and research findings. Also, we dare to express some speculative ideas about the relation between psychodynamics and dynamic brain systems that may not have been welcomed elsewhere. We are very informal and dedicated to supporting interdisciplinary researchers and serious clinicians. We charge nothing and hence we pay no fee to our speakers, but we always take them out for wine and pizza afterward at the Russell Hotel nearby.

Integrating structure and function: looking at the brain in the context of internal psychological processes

Maggie Zellner and David Olds

David Olds

New York City

New York City

David Olds  

Many of us in the neuropsychoanalysis community take a “dual-aspect monist” position (Panksepp, 2005), seeing the brain and the mind as two different perspectives on the same system. We observe the brain from the objective side – for example, looking at its structure (how the neurons are physically organized and connected) or looking at its function (how and when those neurons fire). We observe the mind from the subjective side – perceiving our own mental life or empathizing with the internal mental life of another. But fundamentally these observations are about the same system, complex as it may be. Therefore, understanding the physical dynamics of the brain – its genetic, neurochemical, connective aspects – can be informed by appreciating the subjective dynamics of the mind – its consciousness, wishes, fears, and expressions. And conversely, perspectives on those subjective dynamics can be enriched by an understanding of how physical parameters may constrain or amplify mental processes.

Happily, many researchers and clinicians are starting to move in this direction. Perspectives on brain circuits or neurochemicals do not have to exist in isolation from perspectives on environment or subjective emotional life, as they so often have in the past few decades. In this issue, excellent examples of this development are two articles that address topics – autism spectrum disorder and sexual desire – that are often attributed solely to neurochemical or structural processes. What is productive about the neuropsychoanalytic approach, we suggest, is that the neurochemical and structural components do not have to be rejected in order to also consider the subjective side of things, but rather can be better understood when linked with mental processes, both conscious and unconscious.

The Target Article in this issue, “An integrative model of autism spectrum disorder: ASD as a neurobiological disorder of experienced environmental deprivation, early life stress and allostatic overload” by William Singletary, M.D., is a major contribution to our awareness of the complex, tragic, and still poorly understood phenomenon of autistic spectrum disorder (ASD).

Introductory notes to the psychodynamics of a case of Klüver-Bucy syndrome

Jose Muñoz Zúñiga

Jose Muñoz Zúñiga

Mexico City
Mexico
Neuropsychiatric Unit

Jose Muñoz Zúñiga   *Email: lucesdeeuforia@hotmail.com
Klüver-Bucy, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, psychodynamic phenocopy

Klüver-Bucy syndrome (KBS) is a neuropsychiatric syndrome secondary to damage in anterior temporolimbic structures. It is composed of severe cognitive, behavioral, and affective symptoms. The case of a young woman who developed a KBS after a multiphasic acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is examined. The clinical material is taken from multiple hospitalizations in the Neuropsychiatric Unit of the National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery in Mexico City and from multiple diagnostic interviews with the patient and her family during ambulatory care. A series of correlations will be made between neuropsychiatric symptoms, neuropsychological data, neuroanatomical lesions as shown on neuroimaging, and first-person subjective data. This will be done with the purpose of sketching the psychodynamics of this particular patient while dealing at the same time with relevant issues for the understanding of the inner world of this type of cases. As the patient did not undergo psychoanalytic therapy, any data emerging from this single case study should be taken as introductory in nature. This case points out the need of developing new concepts to describe psychopathological manifestations, as they are understood in metapsychology, when applied to neuropsychiatric patients. In this regard, the term “psychodynamic phenocopy” is proposed.

Basic emotional foundations of social dominance in relation to Panksepp's affective taxonomy

Donné van der Westhuizen and Mark Solms

Mark Solms

Cape Town
South Africa
Department of Psychology

Mark Solms  

social dominance, basic emotions, testosterone, vasopressin, affective neuroscience

An examination of the chemistries and subcortical substrates of social “dominance” behavior has not been systematically reviewed in relation to the primary emotion circuitries described by Panksepp. This is a necessary first step toward untangling the affective foundations of social dominance, in order to determine whether it may legitimately be considered a discrete basic emotion. In this review, several classes of behavior are identified as potential expressions of dominance. They include intermale fighting, intimidation displays, and territorial scent marking. A review of the neurobiological evidence suggests a locus of control of dominance behaviors in a region defined by high density of testosterone and vasopressin (AVP) receptors surrounding the anterior hypothalamus. While many studies report findings regarding the elicitation of dominance behaviors from direct stimulation of these subcortical sites, there is nonetheless a great deal of inconsistency within the literature, as well as overlap with other basic emotion circuitries, making the identification of a consistently recognizable subcortical circuit across species a great challenge. Furthermore, the chemical control of dominance is probably more diverse than previously thought. Testosterone and AVP do not appear to be exclusively involved in dominance. These hormones regulate a variety of social behaviors linked to socio-sexual functioning. In light of these observations, it is unlikely that the coherence observed in the dominance phenotype is attributable to a distinct affective circuit, but it may instead reflect an interaction of several basic emotions operating together as a result of favorable outcomes during social development.

In this bulletin we are pleased to give you the reports of two regional groups who beautifully exemplify the energy and diversity of our Society members. Our colleagues in Israel and Mexico City tell us about an impressive amount of meetings, study groups, and research efforts! You will also see the excellent interdisciplinary outreach that they are engaged in, interacting with colleagues from a wide range of disciplines and introducing ever more people to the rich realm of neuropsychoanalysis.

The Neuropsychoanalysis Group of Mexico City

The main activities of the neuropsychoanalysis group of Mexico City focused on the study group sessions held monthly at Universidad Intercontinental. The topics covered from January to June 2015 have created a dialogue amongst colleagues from different fields, including neurology, psychiatry, psychology and psychoanalysis. The group keeps welcoming new visitors who show enthusiasm about the need of an integration of the neurological and psychodynamic perspectives.

One key development is that the sessions have for the first time included a participant from Colombia through videoconference. This tool has helped to narrow the distance between Spanish-speaking people interested in neuropsychoanalysis.

The sessions from January to April focused on Antonio Damasio's propositions about consciousness, led by Daniela Flores Mosri. The session in May featured the participation of Dr. Ojeda, a neuropsychiatrist from the National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery “Manuel Velasco Suárez.” Dr. Ojeda presented some of the latest findings on dreams and sleep. June included the visit of Arturo Kerbel, a doctoral researcher working at Katerina Fotopoulou's lab at the University College London, and who spoke about anosognosia.

Christian E. Salas

Christian E. Salas

Manchester
UK

Christian E. Salas   *Email: salasriquelme@gmail.com
insula, brain damage, emotion, emotion regulation, lesion studies

Over the past decade, the insula has captured the attention of the scientific community, emerging at the centre of one of most relevant debates of the century: How does the brain generate emotions? Due to its dense connectivity with cortical and subcortical areas that process autonomic and somatic information, researchers have proposed that the insula has a key role in emotional processing. Even though this claim has been supported by neuroimaging studies, we still know little about the potential impact that damage to the insula may have on emotional function. This research digest attempts to offer the reader a brief review of key papers on this topic, thus summarizing the main findings from lesions studies, as well as their theoretical and technical limitations.

Jacqueline Glick

Jacqueline Glick

Jacqueline Glick   glicklee@verizon.net

Reviewed by Jacqueline Glick

Editor's note: This book review was submitted before the recent death of Oliver Sacks; certain references to time have been lightly edited to reflect the fact of his passing. The warmth of Ms. Glick's personal reflections surely resonate with many of us who were touched by Sacks’ writings. In particular, the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society was honored to have Dr. Sacks give opening remarks at our founding congress in London in 2000, and deeply appreciated his public support of the neuropsychoanalytic endeavor. He will be missed.

On February 19th, Dr Oliver Sacks sent the world an announcement through the opinion pages of The New York Times that he had terminal cancer. Accepting this fatal diagnosis, he shared with us what he feels is worth keeping and what can be given up without too much regret in the time he has left. This was the unforgettable backdrop to plunging into reading Sacks’ latest memoir On the move: a life which so forcefully depicts his relentless pursuit of life.

I had also just seen the Charlie Rose program where Rose, Sacks, the painter Chuck Close, and the sculptor Richard Serra discussed “creativity.” With his distinguished white beard, soft voice and head half hidden by his dark blue cap, Sacks portrayed a strikingly different picture on the program than were shown in the photographs on the flap of his book. There we see a handsome, muscled motorbiker — a little rough around the edges. I knew this would be quite a trip. But now I was fearlessly mounting this bike and — hop, on the move, we go.

Before we follow his scientific education along a meandering and difficult personal life, we meet the child: “When I was at boarding school, sent away during the war as a little boy, I had a sense of imprisonment and powerlessness, and I longed for movement and power, ease of movement and superhuman powers.” At this point, we do not get the full force of this moment evoked in his earlier 2001 memoir Uncle Tungsten: Memories of a chemical boyhood, in which he describes how he was beaten almost daily over four years at the hands of a sadistic headmaster. He had been torn away from his safe, warm, attentive parents and wider family. A little boy who had freely experimented and often went too far in his chemical experiments, filling the house with noxious gases! That freedom too had been taken away.

Neuropsychoanalysis has an influence on psychoanalytic technique but not on the psychoanalytic method

Andrea Clarici

Andrea Clarici

Trieste
Italy
Psychiatric Clinic, Department of Medical, Surgical and Health Science

Andrea Clarici   *Email: clarici@units.it
psychoanalytic psychotherapy, neuropsychoanalysis, core psychoanalytic stance

The psychoanalytic method requires, on the analyst's part, a core psychoanalytic stance, where the patient can be reached in a conjoint working-through process, allowing a gradual understanding of the feelings present in the consulting room. Clinical neuropsychoanalysis originated with the presumption that this sort of treatment is valuable for patients suffering from brain lesions. Arising from the practice of clinical neuropsychoanalysis, and responding to critiques of the implications of neuropsychoanalysis in general, the author proposes that neuroscience can positively impact psychoanalysis, but within limits. Specifically, neuroscience provides useful information and conceptual tools that may affect the parameters of treatment – psychoanalytic technique – but can only help indirectly to understand the inner world as the patient subjectively conceives it; in other words, it does not fundamentally impact the basic analytic method. This basic stance, kindled in the analyst by controlled identification with the patient (as exemplified by countertransference-based interpretations), is enhanced by the intrinsic capacity for empathy and introspection, on the part of the psychotherapist and progressively, it is hoped, the patient, even those with neurological impairments. Technique (whether derived from neuroscientific notions or from psychoanalytic theory) can only help to facilitate change in circumstances in which this core psychoanalytic stance is in place. A corollary to this is that, in certain circumstances, theory (be it neurological or psychoanalytic in origin) may even inhibit this crucial psychoanalytic process. This view is supported by revisiting Joseph Sandler's ideas on the “theory of technique” in psychoanalysis and by examples taken from clinical practice with patients with brain injuries.

The Oxford-style debate: the 15th neuropsychoanalysis congress, New York, 2014

“This house believes that neuroscientific terms must never replace psychoanalytic ones”

Daniela Flores Mosri , Ariane Bazan , Nikolai Axmacher , Richard Kessler and Lisa Ouss

Lisa Ouss

Germany
Department of Neuropsychology, Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience

Service de Psychologie Clinique et Différentielle; Centre de Recherhe en Psychologie Clinique

Lisa Ouss  

Following the successful debut of Oxford-style debates in the congresses of Athens and Cape Town, the 15th neuropsychoanalysis congress had its own motion: This house believes that neuroscientific terms must never replace psychoanalytic ones. Moderated by Katerina Fotopoulou, the debate took on one of the biggest discussions in neuropsychoanalysis, which is that of two languages in a dialogue that are thus exposed to mutual influence and updating, but not necessarily to supplanting each other. There are several opinions on the topic, and four colleagues who have been active in the neuroscience-psychoanalysis dialogue for a number of years were asked to share their thoughts. For the motion were Ariane Bazan and Richard Kessler. Against were Lisa Ouss and Nikolai Axmacher. Clinical and research perspectives were represented on both sides of the question: on the “for” side, Kessler is a psychoanalyst, and Bazan is both a biologist and a psychoanalyst; on the “against” side, Lisa Ouss is a child psychiatrist and a psychoanalytic psychotherapist who also conducts research, and Nikolai Axmacher is a cognitive neuroscientist. In this issue, we present essays based on the speakers’ opening statements. Responses will be invited from a range of contributors for online viewing, and selected responses, including those of the original debaters, will appear in a forthcoming issue of the journal.

Daniela Flores Mosri

dannmos@yahoo.com

Speaking to the subject or speaking to the function: each address requires its proper terms

Ariane Bazan

In neuropsychoanalysis, the epistemological line most held is the “dual aspect monism” perspective. This perspective holds that “our brains, including mind, are made of one kind of stuff, cells, but we perceive this stuff in two different ways” (Solms & Turnbull, 2003, pp. 56–58; our italics). One is the neuroscientists’ “objective” way, or the brain, which we dissect “with scalpel and microscope or look at it with brain scans and then trace neurochemical pathways.” The other way is the psychoanalysts’ “subjective” way, or the mind: “how we feel and what we think. Freud refined this kind of observation into free association.” As, however, there is only one object, in the end, there is a more or less direct correspondence between phenomena of the brain and phenomena of the mind.

An integrative model of autism spectrum disorder: ASD as a neurobiological disorder of experienced environmental deprivation, early life stress and allostatic overload

William Singletary

William Singletary

Philadelphia
PA

William Singletary   Email: wsingletarymd@gmail.com
autism, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, allostasis, stress, developmental neurobiology, neuroplasticity

A number of recent convergences within neurobiology, and between neurobiology and psychoanalysis, allow us to view autism through a new lens. This perspective highlights biological risk factors that might operate through final common pathways to produce the ASD syndrome. The goal of this article is to integrate and elaborate upon this confluence of findings, and to develop a working model of ASD that could parsimoniously account for central aspects of ASD, promote greater collaboration in research, and lead to more effective treatment. Converging evidence suggests that ASD is a potentially reversible neurodevelopmental disorder in which neurobiological factors not poor parenting interfere with the childcaregiver interaction. The infant then experiences deprivation of growth-promoting parental input even though it is available. The model proposed here adds what seems to have been largely unrecognized in the field of autism: the child's experience of social deprivation and isolation signals threat to the child and may result in overwhelming stress with significant psychological (traumatic or toxic stress) and biological (allostatic overload) components and consequences. Allostatic overload results when attempts to cope with threat impose too great a burden, resulting in a pathophysiological state or process that damages the body and predisposes one to the development of disease. Critically, this model proposes that allostatic overload plays a major role in the course of ASD by amplifying the neurobiological vulnerabilities generally considered to make primary contributions to the development of autism. Furthermore, through the process of allostatic overload, neurobiological and psychological factors interact in a nonlinear fashion and are both seen to underlie the symptoms of ASD which develop through maladaptive coping and neuroplasticity. Thus, this model might explain both the progression to, and the ongoing symptoms of, the ASD syndrome. In addition, the model could also account for successful intervention by promoting the reversal of this process via adaptive coping and neuroplasticity. Factors that may facilitate adaptive neuroplasticity include providing an enriched environment, increasing social and emotional connection, and decreasing anxiety, stress, and allostatic load. Personal descriptions of the experience of ASD, as well as psychoanalytic clinical work with children with ASD, are in accord with this model. Psychoanalysis may thus be considered a research tool that assists in uncovering the child's inner world of feelings and meanings, an under-appreciated element in autism. Making sense of the child's experience of isolation and threat helps the ASD child feel understood and less afraid. Clinical material will illustrate how, for some children on the higher end of the autism spectrum, recovery is made more likely by increasing the sense of connection and decreasing the experience of stress.

Neuropsychology of cardiovascular disease

Julia Segal

Julia Segal

Julia Segal   juliasegal@mscounselling.com

When my mother was diagnosed with vascular dementia 10 years ago, a well-trained nurse gave her and the family clear, useful information about the condition and its prognosis. When my father had signs of heart failure (HF) this year, no such information was available. Face to face, the consultant told my father that his heart was not failing, although the letter that followed contradicted this. I can only suppose that he did not want to increase my father's evident anxiety, though how we were to account for his symptoms was less clear. Nobody mentioned possible mental or psychological effects, and it was not until I read this book that I realized that my father had a chronic cardiovascular condition which could have accounted for his declining mental state – a decline which worried him enormously but was not acknowledged by any of the doctors he saw.

When most non-medical people think of cardiovascular problems they associate shortness of breath, and difficulties walking long distances or up hills or stairs. They do not associate damage to the brain. If anything, they might have a vague suspicion that the brain protects itself from the impact of cardiovascular problems. This book leaves the reader with a far clearer view. It describes the many ways in which such protection can break down, and gathers together numerous studies which correlate dysfunctions of the cardiovascular system with impairments in the capacities to think, to function, to remember.

Widespread ignorance of these matters is explained by the fact that it is only recently that advances in medication have allowed substantial numbers of people to survive with chronic or mild cardiovascular diseases: in the USA, these are now the leading cause of hospitalization in people older than 65 (p. 410). Amongst this population, estimates of cognitive impairments range from 25% to 75%. It was only 30 years ago that the term “cardiogenic dementia” was introduced, and it is only recently that evidence has emerged that “patients with HF [heart failure] are at an increased risk for cognitive impairment compared to their age-matched peers and patients with other types of cardiovascular disease” (p. 415).
